items.title: These London Apartments Look Straight Out of the Stone Age. Could They Be the Future of Sustainable Architecture?
items.desc: A new residential complex with a load-bearing exoskeleton made from 1,000 tons of raw stone is offering an alternative to carbon-intensive steel and concrete structures. Its designers think that the monumental stone buildings of the past are coming back into fashion
items.text:
From low-carbon concrete to mass timber to green steel , architects across the globe are employing cutting-edge technology to revolutionize eco-friendly building design. But the team behind a new north London apartment complex argues the industry’s path forward may lie in the ways of the past.
With a hulking, pink exoskeleton decorated with Celtic patterns, Petra Heights , a trio of apartment towers ranging from six to 10 stories, looks straight out of the Stone Age . That’s fitting, as the development’s load-bearing structures and decorative cladding are one and the same: stacks of raw, unchiseled stone.
“All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone,” the project’s engineer, Steve Webb , co-founder of engineering firm Webb Yates , tells Dezeen ’s Jennifer Hahn. Altogether, the complex houses a ground-floor storefront, two rooftop gardens and 22 apartments.
Petra Heights is part of an ongoing collaboration between architecture firm Groupwork , headed by Amin Taha , and Webb Yates to popularize stone as a viable alternative to steel and cement, which together represent 16 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.
The stone frame—made of pink basalt from Sicily and larvikite from Norway—produces fewer carbon emissions than traditional steel-and-concrete models. With a stone external frame and a concrete internal frame, the Petra Heights project produced around 30 percent less carbon emissions than a fully steel or concrete alternative, the Guardian ’s Oliver Wainwright reports. Those savings could rise to 95 percent with domestically-mined stone, per Dezeen .
The two men began looking into stone 15 years ago after running into roadblocks while collaborating on a steel frame. A conservation officer pointed them towards stone. Skeptical, they asked a stonemason about the feasibility of building with the material, the Architect's Newspaper ’s Richard Martin reports.
“Are you completely stupid?” Webb recalls the mason saying, according to the Architect’s Newspaper . “Just look around London—it’s been all stone for the last one thousand years. It’s still standing. Of course you can build in stone.”
Since then, they have continually pushed the edge of what stone and wood can do. In 2021, the pair’s six-story 15 Clerkenwell Close , featuring a load-bearing stone structure, was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize , the United Kingdom’s most prestigious architecture award. items.text:
Most people spend their lives trying to avoid getting arrested, but for one 99-year-old woman in the Netherlands, it was a dream come true. In February 2017, a woman named Annie finally got to check an unusual item off her bucket list, thanks to some accommodating local police officers.
While typical bucket list items might include traveling the world or trying an adventurous activity, Annie had a slightly different goal: experiencing what it was like to be locked up in a jail cell. Luckily, she didn’t have to commit a crime to make it happen.
After learning about her aunt’s unusual wish, Annie’s niece reached out to the police department in Nijmegen-Zuid, Netherlands, to see if they could help. Although civilians aren’t normally allowed inside police holding cells, an officer named Maarten decided to make a special exception.
Annie got the full experience, complete with a ride to the police station, handcuffs, and a brief stay behind bars. And judging by the photos shared online, she couldn’t have been happier. The 99-year-old was all smiles as she posed in handcuffs and waved from inside her cell.
Of course, Annie wasn’t actually in trouble with the law, and the entire experience was arranged just for her. Still, it’s safe to say that she got a taste of life on the other side of the bars, without having to worry about a criminal record.
It just goes to show that you’re never too old to try something new, even if that something happens to be getting arrested.

items.text:
The largest fleet of electric school buses in New York State is up and running in a South Bronx neighborhood where childhood asthma rates are more than twice the national average.
Family-owned school bus company GVC has served schoolchildren with special needs in the Bronx for more than 30 years, and the company worked over the summer to install 23 dual‑port chargers to power 45 new electric school buses.
The buses will collectively prevent the emission of 1 million pounds of emissions per school year. Exhaust pollutants like carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and fine particulate matter pose serious threats to residents’ long-term pulmonary health, including through elevated asthma risk, and those most at risk are passengers waiting for buses and sitting on buses—the schoolchildren included.
GVC’s bus depot is located on Zerega Avenue, along a 2-mile corridor where around 2,000 school buses and 3,000 medium and heavy-duty vehicles pass every day.
“The children we transport are especially vulnerable to air and noise pollution,” Michael Townsend, Compliance Officer at GVC, said in a statement.
“Transitioning our fleet to electric is making a difference in people’s lives. The children we transport, and all those who live and work in the area, are enjoying cleaner air and quieter streets.”
Con Edison, one of New York’s largest utilities, worked with GVC from the earliest stages of their bus fleet transition, upgrading the grid to handle the demand from the bus chargers, offering a $450,000 incentive , and identifying other avenues of support from the city and state governments that could accelerate the transition.
This included the New York School Bus Incentive Program (NYSBIP) funded by the Clean Water, Clean Air, and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act. The NYSBIP helped fund 20 of GVC’s electric buses and the 23 dual-port chargers.

items.title: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild
items.desc: Two nests were spotted in September, and authorities moved the eggs to an aquarium to protect them from an incoming tropical storm. Over the weekend, dozens of hatchlings emerged and have now been released on the same beaches where they were found
items.text:
In September, authorities in California were baffled to find two sea turtle nests on their beaches—the first natural ones ever confirmed on the United States’ West Coast. Now, dozens of the eggs have hatched. Experts released the baby olive ridley turtles over the weekend, allowing the tiny creatures to begin their perilous journeys to adulthood.
The two nests were identified on Seal Beach and Huntington Beach in Orange County. Because a tropical storm was coming soon after the nests were found, biologists moved the more than 200 eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific. The Ping-Pong ball-size spheres stayed in closed incubators under sand in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, simulating their ideal natural conditions.
Aquarium staff first saw signs of hatching activity on November 12, when they noticed changes in the surface of the sand in the incubation container with the Seal Beach eggs, said Lance Adams , the aquarium’s veterinarian, during a press conference on November 14. The team spotted a depression and some cracks in the sand, indicating something was happening beneath it. The first turtle emerged the following day at around 7:15 p.m. Pacific time. Around two hours later, more of the baby turtles from the Seal Beach nest started popping out, resulting in 54 squirming critters.
“It kind of went from looking like very smooth beach sand to looking like an eruption of baby sea turtles,” Adams explained. It “was really exciting and very, very cute.” As of the press conference date, 50 eggs from the nest had not hatched. Experts do not know whether they’re viable, but they will continue monitoring the makeshift home.
The Seal Beach hatchlings were released in the same location where their nest had been, very early on Saturday morning, before the sun had risen, according to a social media post . That’s because baby turtles use moonlight to navigate toward the ocean. After reaching the water, hatchlings experience a “frenzy period” in which they swim continuously for 24 to 48 hours, according to the post. The energetic outburst is justified; experts estimate that only one in 1,000 olive ridley turtle hatchlings survive to adulthood, according to a statement .

items.text:
A post shared by Save the Chimps (@savethechimps)
Heavy rain and rising floodwaters in Florida made parts of Save the Chimps sanctuary inaccessible. As a result, staff had to get creative to keep one of their residents supplied. Their solution was a drone, which delivered food and blankets to Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee whose outdoor area had become cut off by the water.
Between November 1 and November 3, 2026, nearly 19 inches of rain fell across the area surrounding the 150-acre sanctuary near Fort Pierce, Florida. The downpour overwhelmed nearby canals, sending water across internal roads and making it difficult for employees to reach the chimpanzees. Staff typically use golf carts to transport approximately 3,000 pounds of food around the property each day, but submerged roads made those routes impassable. A high-clearance swamp buggy initially helped employees navigate the water, but it soon broke down, forcing the team to find alternative ways to get supplies where they were needed.
Fortunately, the sanctuary had purchased a delivery drone some time earlier for emergencies just like this. Staff put it to use when they realized Kaleb became isolated in an outdoor area surrounded by floodwater. The drone carried food and blankets to him until he eventually moved on his own to a more accessible part of the property.
Footage shared by the sanctuary showed Kaleb retrieving a paper bag dropped by the drone and pulling out a banana. Luckily, he and the sanctuary’s more than 200 chimpanzees remained safe thanks to the dedication of the staff who stayed overnight to ensure the animals continued receiving care. According to the sanctuary’s facilities director, the chimpanzees continued receiving their food on schedule.
By November 7, water levels had dropped considerably, although only about 20% of the property’s roads were passable. The sanctuary has since begun assessing the damage, which includes roads requiring extensive resurfacing, damaged vehicles and equipment, and buildings in need of roof repairs and mold remediation.
Save the Chimps is now appealing to donors for help covering the recovery costs, with one supporter agreeing to match contributions. While the flooding temporarily complicated nearly every aspect of the sanctuary’s daily operations, its emergency preparations helped ensure that the chimpanzees remained safe and cared for throughout the storm.

items.title: SpaceX Catches the Upper Stage of Its Starship for the First Time, Making the Company One Step Closer to a Reusable Rocket
items.desc: After circling the Earth 14 times, the upper portion of Starship descended to the planet's surface and was caught by a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms. However, the company failed to snatch the lower stage, which it had previously demonstrated
items.text:
On November 14, SpaceX successfully caught the separated upper section of its massive Starship rocket as it returned from Earth orbit, marking a historic step toward the development of reusable rockets.
“That was the missing link,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during a livestream of the landing, reports Mike Wall at Space.com . “That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes.”
The 407-foot rocket launched for its 15th test flight from the company’s Starbase site in southern Texas on November 13. The lower stage, called the Super Heavy booster, separated during the ascent after providing the thrust needed for takeoff. The upper stage, called the Starship spacecraft, went on to complete a roughly 22.5-hour journey, which involved 14 laps around Earth and the deployment of 26 Starlink satellites.
After that, the spacecraft navigated back to Starbase, where a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms captured it.
“Can you believe it?” Huot said during the livestream, reports Marcia Dunn for the Associated Press . “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”

This time around, the booster had to be diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico because of low fuel. SpaceX is investigating what triggered the issue, according to a statement .
Still, snatching the upper stage is harder than grabbing the booster, since the Starship spacecraft travels higher and faster than the lower stage, according to Space.com . The historic catch brings SpaceX closer to its goal of building a fully reusable rocket. The company wants to build a rocket system that can travel to space and back with minimal refurbishments needed between launches.

items.desc: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? items.text:
About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?
B rett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.
“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”
Gout has been with us for as long as we know: in 1910 a case was diagnosed in a mummy found near a temple in Upper Egypt. It is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis – and, it is often said, the only curable one – resulting from raised levels of uric acid in the blood. Uric acid is produced when your metabolism breaks down molecules called purines, which are found in your body’s own cells and in certain foods you eat. Excess uric acid is normally processed by the kidneys and passed through urine, but persistently high urate levels can eventually lead to sharp crystals forming in the joints. The presence of these crystals can in turn trigger a profound immune response: inflammation, redness and pain. Eventually, hardened lumps of urate crystals called tophi can form under the skin.
High urate levels can have many causes, but they are not, in themselves, the sole cause of gout. “Virtually all people with gout will have a raised urate level,” says consultant rheumatologist Prof Edward Roddy. “But most people with a raised urate level don’t get gout.”
The pain of a gout attack is so debilitating that it can be hard to describe: the 19th-century writer and clergyman Sydney Smith said it felt “like walking on my eyeballs”. “Sometimes people think they’ve broken a bone – that’s quite a common thing,” says Roddy. “There is some qualitative research showing that people compare the intensity of the pain to having a heart attack or a kidney stone, and that women with gout compare the intensity of the pain to childbirth.”
It can also arrive, in the first instance, with little or no warning. “Often it comes on overnight,” says Roddy. “So somebody goes to bed pain-free, then they wake up and can’t put their foot to the floor.”

items.text:
During a Major League Baseball game between the Kansas City Royals and the Toronto Blue Jays, the best team performance didn’t take place on the field. Instead, it happened in the stands, where fans from all walks of life came together for a mouthwatering mission. All they had to do was to assemble an oversized, inflatable hot dog in a race against time.
The contest, known as “Home Bun Race,” was set up by QuickTrip, a chain of convenience stores in Midwestern, Southern, and Western United States. The objective is for fans in attendance to piece together a 10-foot-tall inflatable hot dog and equally sized bun, which were each launched from opposite sides of the stadium. If the crowd managed to unite the massive meal in under 35 seconds, there would be free hot dogs for everyone.
Though it sounds pretty straight forward, it can be tricky to coordinate and move the inflatable pieces in such a short amount of time—especially when it’s a crowd of strangers who haven’t prepared or ever worked together before. Still, the fans managed to achieve their goal, resulting in a World Series-level roar from the crowd. Although the home team lost 4-3, the fans walked away with a coupon that they could later redeem for their free treat. So… everyone won.
According to Ads of the World , QuickTrip created this campaign in partnership with Laughlin Constable, their creative and media agency. It is also the first activation of its kind in MLB, and the most successful social activation QuickTrip has ever done due to its social media reach and press coverage. In addition to Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City, the campaign has also taken place at the Cardinals stadium in St. Louis.

items.title: 98 Silly, Chaotic, And Accidentally Hilarious Signs People Found In The Wild
items.desc: We’ve gathered some of the more creative and hilarious examples of signs that folks online have found in the wild and decided to share, from puns that your dad would love, to warnings that raise more questions than they answer.
items.text:
Before a sign can be funny, it has to be readable, and that is where most of the science lives. Researchers who reviewed decades of studies on sign visibility point to strong contrast between letters and background as a major factor, and some city design guidelines they cite recommend keeping messages to eight words or fewer.
A sign only gets a couple of seconds of attention, so big letters, a clear color split and a short message are the unglamorous foundation under every memorable one. Even the silliest sign on this list had to pass that test first, otherwise nobody would have stopped long enough to take the photo.
Rhythm helps too, and nobody understood that better than the folks behind Burma Shave. Starting in the 1920s, the shaving cream company posted short messages on a row of roadside signs so drivers could read one line at a time and wait for the punchline at the end. The Minnesota Historical Society notes that early sets did not rhyme, and that shorter rhyming jingles soon followed because motorists could read them more easily.
Over 33 years, more than 6,000 sets went up across 45 states, and the company even ran contests that pulled in tens of thousands of entries in some years. Many of those jingles doubled as safety reminders, including one nudging drivers to be alive when they arrive. Suspense, rhyme and a payoff turned a stretch of highway into entertainment.
Then there is the sweet spot between wrong and harmless. Psychologists Caleb Warren and Peter McGraw, who proposed what they call the benign violation theory , argue that something strikes us as funny when it seems wrong but also feels safe. Signs are practically built for this. They are supposed to be calm, official and a little dull, so when one pleads with the neighborhood about something wildly specific or states the obvious with total confidence, our brains notice the gap between the serious format and the strange message. Nobody is harmed, which means we are free to laugh.

items.title: Women Share 68 Reasons Having A Husband Isn’t Always The Life Upgrade They Expected
items.desc: Marriage is supposed to make life easier, but some husbands seem to have a talent for doing the exact opposite. From conveniently forgetting how to handle basic household chores and leaving their wives with the mental load of running a home to turning minor everyday habits into endless sources of frustration, these seemingly small behaviors can make married life feel like an unpaid second job. items.text:
Marriage often comes with the expectation that two people will share responsibilities and make everyday life easier for each other. However, that arrangement can become frustrating when one partner seems unable to handle even the simplest household tasks. According to Psychology Today , husbands who struggle with cooking, cleaning, scheduling appointments, or managing family responsibilities are not necessarily incapable of doing these things.
Their difficulties can stem from how they were raised, the expectations they grew up with, and the habits they have developed over time. Men who were raised in households where women handled most domestic responsibilities, for example, may have had fewer opportunities to learn these skills or develop confidence in managing a home independently.
Traditional gender roles can also influence how husbands approach household responsibilities, even if they do not consciously believe that certain chores belong to women. Some may simply be less aware of everything involved in maintaining a home , from keeping track of groceries to remembering appointments and organizing family schedules.
Others become accustomed to waiting until their wives ask them to do something, especially when they know someone will eventually step in and handle it. Fear of criticism can also discourage them from taking initiative, while procrastination and deliberately avoiding unpleasant tasks can make it seem as though they are less capable than they really are.
In more extreme situations, repeatedly doing chores poorly or claiming an inability to complete them can become a way of avoiding responsibility altogether.
This imbalance is closely connected to what the BBC describes as the mental load, the invisible cognitive work involved in keeping a household running. It goes beyond physically completing chores and includes noticing what needs attention, planning ahead, remembering important dates, organizing schedules, and making sure everyone has what they need.
Research cited by the BBC found that mothers in one survey of 3,000 American parents handled 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort. This can mean that even when husbands participate in household chores, their wives may still be responsible for remembering what needs to be done and making sure nothing gets overlooked.

items.text:
Some of the “very last wild and healthy ecosystems” unblemished by humans have been discovered in the remote atolls of the Pacific Ocean teeming with life.
Scientists wrote in a new study that, although humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, a few very remote islands of coral may be the exceptions.
Researchers described the two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located in the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.
The two atolls—roughly midway between Hawaii and the Philippines—are now part of a newly created National Marine Sanctuary.
“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” said study first author Dr. Alan Friedlander.
Bikar and Bokak are the northernmost atolls in the Marshall Islands, lying around 72 and 239 miles from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.
The research team in 2023 began conducting extensive monitoring of local land, sea, and sky ecosystems, assessing sea- and shorebird populations, and vegetation.
They conducted surveys of turtle nesting, coral reefs and fish assemblages using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea camera deployments, and a submarine.
Dr. Friedlander, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i, says the extensive surveying of the ecosystems offers an unparalleled glimpse into how they function with only minimal human influence.
Two years after the assessment, some 18,500 square miles around the atolls were declared the country’s first national marine sanctuary.
“These atolls have extensive seabird colonies, mature native vegetation, active turtle nesting, high fish numbers with large predators… and surprisingly diverse and poorly-known deep-sea communities.”
For instance, they counted over a dozen breeding seabird colonies, 266 groups of reef fish, 79 groups of deep-sea fishes, and 15 groups of open-water predators—including sharks, jacks, and wahoo.
Fully 14 of the observed groups haven’t previously been recorded in the Marshall Islands, and two might be species new to science.

People often find ways to get around rules without actually breaking them. Sometimes, they just interpret instructions differently than intended. Even a simple request can leave space for creative interpretation, letting someone follow the words but ignore the real purpose. So why do we look for these loopholes?
This behavior depends on knowing what someone wants, noticing unclear instructions, and seeing where rules can be interpreted differently. Researchers from MIT and Harvard say these deliberate misunderstandings are common in daily life, showing how people can take advantage of gaps between what is said and what is meant.
This explains why finding everyday loopholes can feel rewarding: the person isn’t breaking a rule, just finding another way to follow it. Still, not every clever workaround means bending the rules. Sometimes, people just figure out how to get more value from systems meant to reward them.
Credit card rewards can turn regular purchases into airline miles , cashback, or points for other benefits. Customers who know how these programs work can get a lot of value from sign-up bonuses and rewards. Some even plan their spending to make the most of these perks, rather than just using any card to pay.

Research on the US credit card market found that people who understand finances make money from reward cards, while less-informed cardholders lose out. These programs also encourage more spending, which can leave some people with bigger unpaid balances and extra interest charges.

Those who carry balances might pay much more than they get back. This leads to another question: when does using a system become crossing the line?

The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.
ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The mission will examine the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) collision, helping scientists better understand how the technique could one day be used to protect Earth from incoming space rocks.
The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter. They form a binary asteroid system , a pair of asteroids that are gravitationally bound, orbiting each other around a shared center of mass.
In September 2022, the golf-cart-size DART spacecraft intentionally struck the smaller celestial body in the world’s first demonstration of asteroid deflection technology. The mission not only successfully collided with Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around its big sibling by 33 minutes; it also altered the asteroid pair’s route around the sun . Now, Hera is returning to the crash scene to follow up on that work.
“Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene,” Patrick Michel , a planetary scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research and Hera’s principal investigator, tells Meghan Bartels for Space.com .
The spacecraft, which is about the size of a small car , performed its first arrival maneuver on October 15, and ESA released Hera’s first close-up photo of the asteroid duo on November 5. The picture, snapped about 37 miles from the rocky pair, prominently features Didymos, with the smaller Dimorphos mostly hidden in the larger asteroid’s shadow.
While looking at this image, “the first thing we said was wow!” Michel says in a statement . “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.”
On November 12, ESA released another image of the asteroid system , this time taken from about 35 miles away. It shows one side of Didymos and a sliver of Dimorphos peeking out from behind the larger rock, on the upper left. This photo reveals various features on the bigger asteroid’s surface, including large boulders, smooth areas and a sharp ridge at the equator.

Unconventional wedding venues can delight and surprise guests—and even the couple. While they may take more planning than a commonly used space (like a church or banquet hall), they often deliver striking visual impact and serve as a unique metaphor for love and devotion. Couple Nara Kim and Yoorim held their nuptials in a rice paddy in Hoengseong, Gangwon-do, South Korea. Part wedding, part art installation , it was all a celebration of love. Photographer Kyungho Lee immortalized the special day in stunning imagery.
The idea to marry in a rice paddy grew out of how Kim and Yoorim viewed their relationship. “The eight years the couple spent together were likened to the process of cultivating the land, sowing seeds, and finally reaping a harvest,” an Instagram post from Ryohan , their wedding director, explains. “Inspired by this, they envisioned a wedding in a rice paddy; after searching for a suitable location for about a month, they ultimately chose this spot in Hoengseong.”
The wedding setup featured long tables centered in the rice paddy clearing. Just beyond one table was the ceremony site, marked by a sculptural backdrop of cascading, braided rice straw punctuated by a variety of flowers. When not in use, the piece served as both art and a monument to Kim and Yorrim’s love.
The ceremony space was prepared by harvesting the rice grown there with a tractor, and the crop became part of the wedding itself. “[The harvested rice] was used to prepare food and tteok (traditional rice cakes) for the guests, while bags of the rice were given as wedding favors—a gesture symbolizing the sharing of the couple’s hard-earned harvest,” Ryohan shares. “Every step of the wedding—from the rice growing in the paddy to its appearance on the guests’ dining tables—was woven into a single, cohesive narrative. items.text:
Video games get a bad rap. Though they’re often looked down upon as a distracting outlet for young adults, despite the creativity and problem-solving that’s often involved, it turns out they can also be essential in saving lives. Teenager Kylie Arellano was rescued after allegedly being held captive for more than 500 days, thanks to an unlikely connection she made with another player through the popular online game Among Us .
An online multiplayer game that uses social deduction to seek out the “impostors” in a group of players, Among Us rose in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic and served as a great way for friends to keep in touch during quarantine. For Arellano, who went missing from her Utah home in May 2025, the game’s ability to connect players with one another ultimately became a crucial part of her rescue.
Arellano was allegedly held captive in the basement of 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel’s home in Huntington, Oregon. Although Harmel had reportedly taken away her original phone, he eventually gave her another device that could connect to Wi-Fi but had no cellular service. This allowed Arellano to play Among Us and, more importantly, communicate with other people through the game.
In mid-October 2026, Arellano began talking with another player she met while playing Among Us . Their conversations eventually moved to another social media platform, where she revealed her identity and explained that she was being held against her will. The other player (a child) told their mother, who contacted the FBI.
On November 1, the FBI monitored a video call between Arellano and the other player’s family, during which she shared details about her situation. Authorities were able to rescue her from the Oregon home that same day. Harmel was subsequently charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
While Among Us was originally designed as a way for players to work together and identify hidden impostors, for Arellano, it became something much more important. The game provided her with a way to reach the outside world, ultimately helping bring her captivity to an end.

items.title: 43 Times People Were Humbled By Their Own Old Posts (New Pics)
items.desc: Somewhere in the archive, your old opinions are waiting for their moment. These are the people who found out the hard way, halfway through an ill-advised rant, when a stranger scrolled back a few years and dropped a screenshot with two words attached: "Is that you?" Politicians and keyboard warriors alike got to debate their own timelines and lose. The internet forgets nothing, and its timing is i
items.text:
Most people who get an "Is that you?" reply aren't lying when they insist they've always believed what they're saying now. Their memory has been wired to edit itself. In 1973, psychologists George Goethals and Richard Reckman measured students' opinions on school busing, then put them in group discussions where planted participants argued the opposite side.
Many students changed their minds. When asked to recall what they had originally thought, they remembered their old views as much closer to their new ones than they actually were. Their brains rewrote the draft and deleted the evidence, but these days a screenshot is happy to restore it.
Even people who remember their position will bend it when it's convenient. In 1997, Daniel Batson and his colleagues at the University of Kansas gave participants two tasks to hand out, one with a pleasant outcome and one dull. They were told the fair way to decide was a coin flip. Some participants flipped, and about 90% of those still gave themselves the better task, whatever the coin said. Batson called it moral hypocrisy, the urge to look fair without paying the price of being fair.
Spotting it in other people is the easy part. In 2002, Princeton psychologist Emily Pronin and her colleagues found that people rate themselves as less biased than the average person, a pattern they named the bias blind spot . Your own opinion feels like common sense, and someone else's feels like an agenda. That's why the scroll-back reply feels so good to write and so bad to receive.
Politicians learned long ago that voters keep score. In March 2004, John Kerry tried to explain a vote on funding for the Iraq war and landed on, "I actually did vote for the $87 billion before I voted against it." The Bush campaign put the line in an ad, and "flip-flopper" followed him through the rest of the race. Eight years later, Mitt Romney's adviser Eric Fehrnstrom told CNN that the general election was "almost like an Etch A Sketch. You can kind of shake it up, and we start all over again." His primary rivals quickly turned the toy into a campaign prop.

A new generation of trash bins are aimed at conserving Japanese civic culture while addressing one of the country’s largest tourism headaches.
Solar-powered compactors and robots that haul trash away from key tourist areas are two such solutions already receiving a positive response.
If you’ve ever visited Japan, you too may have been left confused and eventually frustrated by what appears to be a total absence of public waste bins. This is by design.
Officials concerned about security and overflowing bins have left the public with few places to dispose of their trash. There is also a philosophy that if waste is difficult to dispose of, people will be less prone to creating it.
Japanese tourism authorities are beginning to understand that, while this approach may have seen citizens keep their streets clean for decades, it’s a major inconvenience for visitors.
Yet the trend towards removing waste bins has continued, with the Tokyo metro removing all public waste bins as recently as 2022. In parallel, however, the city has been enlisting the help of various firms to design smarter waste bins that hold more and won’t overflow.
One example is Forcetec, which sells and installs solar-powered waste bins developed in the United States called SmaGO. It compacts waste every 5 minutes and can hold 5 times as much trash as a non-compacting bin.
“There are many places that recognize the need for trash bins but hesitate to install them because they’re worried the bins will overflow or because of the labor required to collect the rubbish,” says Rina Ogata, a spokesperson for Forcetec.
“You can install SmaGO and reduce the frequency of rubbish collection. The communications function also allows operators to check online how full each bin is, so they can make collections more efficiently before the bins reach capacity.”
Companies like Forcetec have donated or subsidized these products as part of “a corporate hometown tax program” and “corporate sponsorships” according to Japan Times .
Another reason why cities like Kyoto and Tokyo decided to trash their trash cans was that they fill up too quickly in busy areas, and collection of each bin was an expensive outlay.
But what if the trash cans could collect themselves? Enter California-based firm Cartken , whose 40-liter robotic trash bins use sensors to measure when they’re almost full, at which point they drive themselves out of the public reach for emptying.

From the sun-soaked plains of Parma comes the story of an Italian farmer who accidentally brought on a Biblical resurrection with very modern implications for our food system.
Claudio Grossi doubted whether the shriveled wheat seeds he found in his attic would grow into anything.
Grossi threw the seeds into a pile of manure, curious to see what might come of it. Soon, he found wheat stalks that towered over his commercial wheat crop, and instead of sprouting one ear, these stalks sprouted seven.
The pattern of those 7 ears proved important. One tall ear was surrounded by 6 thin ears of different colors. Grossi had spent his whole life farming wheat and had never heard of anything like it.
Smithsonian Magazine’s Lina Zeldovich wrote that he could find nothing about it in any agricultural manuals, a clue as to the “freak” grain’s origin did indeed come from a Good Book.
“And behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good,” read a page in the Book of Genesis that Grossi happened upon one Sunday in church. 7 ears, one stalk, just like the “freak of nature” at his farm.
Indeed, what his great-grandfather grew after he bought the farm in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region in 1915 was an ancient form of wheat called Triticum turgidum convar. compositum, as scientists at the University of Parma would later determine. It evolved in Türkiye, Egypt, and other countries along the Mediterranean, and was cultivated one upon a time in Italy.
As a commercial grain, its production declined around the time of the Mussolini dictatorship because its impressive height made it vulnerable to snapping under wind, heavy rains, and hailstorms before the grains would mature.
Additionally, dough made from T. turgidum flour doesn’t leaven well, and unusual preparations need to be made for baking with it.
Yet one by one, the positives which Grossi experienced made him wonder why Italian farmers ever stopped cultivating it. Tall, large, and hardy, it overshadows weeds, shows resistance to drought, and appears less reliant on fertilizer than other breeds. Grossi began calling it his “Miracle Wheat” or grano del miracolo.

In 1994, David vacationed on the Greek island of Kos with his family for a memorable week in which the English teen met a new pen pal.
There were 12 kids, all from different families, that became a friendly pack. One of them was Jodie, who was 15 at the time.
“You know how kids hang out on holiday, we were all just around the pool table and we decided to swap addresses and be pen pals.”
“Me and Jodie were the only ones that stayed in contact—and we carried on writing to each other for years. A letter every month or so, catching up.”
But after three years of communication, David moved, and the pair lost contact.
Little did they know that 29 years later they would get married.
David McArdle from Newcastle was two years older than Jodie, and they both went on their separate life paths.
It wasn’t until twenty years later that David saw a text message arrive on his mother’s phone from Jodie, saying ‘Happy birthday from me and the girls’.
“I couldn’t believe I found her again,” David told Talk to the Press. “I said to my mum, ‘I didn’t know you had Jodie’s number.’”
He replied to the text immediately (saying it was David) and, after a nail-biting 15-minute wait, Jodie, a teaching assistant, messaged back.
“She said she was so glad to hear from me.
“It turns out, that 15-minute wait for her reply was because she was sobbing her heart out looking at the text. She’d wanted to get in touch, but she thought I was in a relationship so she didn’t want to ruffle any feathers.”
From then on, the two never stop talking on the phone for two years, before eventually meeting in person, for the first time in 24 years, when David drove 300 miles to Cardiff to visit Jodie.
“We sat on the sofa and talked for 12 hours,” recalled David who visited her again two weeks later.
After three years of dating, David proposed at the top of the London Eye Ferris wheel and the pair were soon married.
Now the couple live together in Cardiff but visit Kos, the island they met on, every year in August, back to the apartments where they met and swapped addresses.

Jersey primary school children have enjoyed learning about space in a lesson delivered by an astronomer.
Dr Robin Catchpole of the Cambridge Institute of Astronomy was invited to the island by the Jersey Astronomy Club and shared his extensive knowledge with pupils aged 10 and 11 at First Tower School.
Year 6 pupil Lola, 11, said her favourite part was learning about how the planets were created while Vihaan, 10, said he was fascinated by black holes and how they were formed.
Catchpole, who has written and co-written more than 100 research papers and articles on astronomy, said his trick for making space accessible to children was to show them planets they would be familiar with.
Catchpole said he first became interested in astronomy when his grandfather gave him a book about the subject and his mother showed him the Moon through a telescope on the beachfront in Torquay, Devon.
"I saw craters and shadows of mountains and I thought that was very exciting," he said.
Year 6 teacher Lee Bradshaw said it was a great opportunity to have an expert like Catchpole answering questions and children proved inquisitive about the subject.

The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.
In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.
Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.
But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
The lives of artists Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell —collaborators, companions and sometimes lovers—were deeply intertwined both on canvases and in private quarters.
The pair were central figures in the Bloomsbury Group , a circle of artists and intellectuals active in early 20th-century Britain who radically, and often controversially, challenged contemporary creative and social norms. These included public sentiments on philosophy, sexuality and mental illness. The group featured, among others, the economist John Maynard Keynes , as well as the writers E. M. This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA 's Voyager 1 probe , which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.
While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and " Solar System Family Portrait " images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.
One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter . From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system 's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA . As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.
Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes , which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

items.desc: Researchers collected the mushroom from a moss-covered palm trunk in the central Florida wetland. Its relatives are known to produce amatoxins, but the fungus surprisingly turned blue when handled, a telltale sign that the organism makes psilocybin
items.text:
A little brown mushroom that grows in the swamps of Florida offers a lethal two-for-one deal: It can get you high and kill you.
The fungus Galerina indica , dubbed the “dark magic mushroom,” produces both the mind-altering chemicals psilocybin and psilocin, as well as deadly amatoxins, making it the first species of mushroom known to contain both types of compounds. The findings, published in the journal Current Biology on November 11, offer new understanding of the evolution and diversity of fungi.
“Humanity’s cultural infatuation with mushrooms has long been bookended by two categories: mushrooms that induce psychedelic experiences and mushrooms that are deadly toxic,” says study co-author Andrew Kunik , a fungal biologist who conducted the research at the University of Florida, to Ed Cara at Gizmodo . “Our discovery of the ‘dark magic mushroom’ represents an unusual convergence of worlds, where we now know of this rare and unusual species that produces the chemistry responsible for both properties.”
Some mushrooms are known to contain either psilocybin or amatoxins, and the latter is well-documented in certain Galerina fungi. G. indica , however, is a less-studied variety. Kunik spotted the unassuming species on a moss-covered palm trunk while studying fungi in the wetland of central Florida in 2025. Surprisingly, the specimen turned blue when handled—a sign that it might produce psilocybin.
So, Kunik and colleagues conducted chemical analyses of the mushroom, along with specimens of two unnamed Galerina species collected in the southeastern United States between January 2024 and September 2025. The work revealed that G. indica contained psilocybin, psilocin and two amatoxins, including a toxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. One of the other Galerina species they studied had only the psychedelic substances, while the other made neither type of compound.
“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle , a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the work, to Tina Hesman Saey at Science News .
The largest G. indica mushrooms found stood around 0.2 inches tall and had caps up to roughly 0.1 inches wide, according to Live Science .

items.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
items.desc: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
items.text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.
At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.
To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes.

items.title: Ancient Humans May Have Hunted Hippos With Poisoned Spear Tips on the Arabian Peninsula 125,000 Years Ago
items.desc: A new study suggests people hunted and processed game near a large, lush, freshwater lake in what is now southern Saudi Arabia, challenging the assumption that humans just passed through the region
items.text:
Today, southern Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry desert, with sand dunes as far as the eye can see. But 125,000 years ago, it was home to a lush, freshwater lake that supported animals like hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles and oryx.
A new study, published November 12 in the journal Science , suggests that ancient humans took advantage of this rich biodiversity—and may even have created poisoned weapons to take down their prey.
Researchers conducted excavations at a Middle Paleolithic site known as Uruq Aljelibah, which means “sand dunes of a watering hole.” It’s located in the Empty Quarter, or Rub' al-Khali , a vast desert region spanning southern Saudi Arabia, as well as parts of Yemen, Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The evidence suggests the site was once home to a 131-square-mile lake that measured nearly 100 feet deep and was surrounded by palms, reeds, trees, shrubs and other plants, per a statement .
While investigating the site, archaeologists discovered more than 500 fossilized animal remains and more than 5,500 stone tools and artifacts, including stone points they think may have been dipped in poison to paralyze or kill big game.
The weapons were clustered near animal bones, which suggests the lakeshore was used for hunting and processing game. They also showed damage consistent with striking large animals, and some still had microscopic traces of animal tissue near their tips. Several also had chemical biomarkers associated with the arrow-poison tree ( Acokanthera schimperi ), a plant that contains cardiac glycosides , naturally occurring compounds that can affect heart rate.
The researchers also found hints of resin and fibers at the bases of the stone points, which suggests they were “hafted”—composite weapons made from multiple materials, rather than simple handheld tools.
“Hafting is often inferred indirectly, based on size and shape of stone tools, for instance,” study co-author Huw Groucutt , an archaeologist at the University of Malta, tells Haaretz ’s Ruth Schuster. “What we have done is find direct evidence in the form of residues showing how the tools were hafted and used, at a scale that is rarely applied in archaeology, and certainly not at sites like this, open air sites in arid regions.”
The scientists also discovered evidence of cutting, scraping and fiber processing, which suggests the people living here were exploiting plant resources for food, tools and binding materials.

items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Ahead of a new exhibition celebrating the portraiture of famed Netherlandish painter Jan van Eyck , a new theory has emerged about one of the artist’s most famous—and deeply puzzling—canvases.
At first glance, the scene in van Eyck’s 1434 Arnolfini Portrait seems straightforward: A man, dressed in black, and woman, clad in green, stand at the center of a lavish room where every detail—furniture, a dog, jewelry, oranges—is placed as though to purposefully highlight their wealth. But a closer look at the space’s geometry offers more uncanny observations. There is no fireplace, as would have been expected, and the ceiling is too low to realistically accommodate the chandelier that nonetheless dangles above their heads. Meanwhile, a convex mirror on the far back wall reveals that the pair are not alone; two figures are entering the room. The man in black lifts his hand, apparently in silent greeting, while a large inscription beside his head reads, in Latin: “Jan van Eyck was here 1434.”
Of all the details in the piece, which borders on the surreal, the identity of the man has been speculated upon the most. The leading theory derives from the 16th century, when inventory records labeling the painting as “hernoul le fin” were interpreted to be the French spelling of “Arnoul fin,” or “Arnolfini,” the surname of a wealthy Italian merchant clan who lived and worked in Bruges, Belgium, where van Eyck kept his studio.
For centuries, many art historians have supported this understanding, considering the piece to be a portrait of some members of that family. Some scholars identify the man as Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini, while others think it depicts his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini. A Catholic health care system in the American Midwest has successfully completed the world’s first reported bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease.
Doctors at Franciscan Health used bone marrow recovered from a deceased organ donor to treat a 40-year-old woman with aplastic anemia
The patient, with a decade-long history of the disease, received the bone marrow stem cell transplant on April 18, after her disease progressed from stable to severe, despite multiple lines of therapy.
Because her disease no longer responded to medication, her care team pursued a transplant to replace her failing marrow with healthy blood-forming stem cells.
Six months after the transplant, the donor marrow has taken hold and restored her blood counts.
She no longer needs blood or platelet transfusions and has achieved full donor chimerism, meaning her blood and immune system are now produced entirely by the donor’s stem cells, without complications.
For non-malignant conditions including severe aplastic anemia, sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia, and other inherited or acquired bone marrow failure disorders, bone marrow-derived stem cells are widely regarded as the preferred stem cell source over peripheral blood stem cells (PBSCs), and the source of choice for non-malignant diseases.
“Bone marrow transplantation for severe aplastic anemia has been performed since the 1970s using living related and unrelated donors.
“To our knowledge, this is the first reported transplant of deceased organ donor bone marrow for severe aplastic anemia,” said Felix Mensah, MD, the treating physician at Franciscan Health.
“This case shows why continued innovation in transplant medicine matters, and why we need more donor options, so that every patient with a life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder has access to potentially curative therapy.”
“Reaching the first non-malignant transplant is a defining moment,” said Kevin Caldwell , Co-Founder and CEO of Ossium, which maintains a marrow bank.
“By recovering and banking bone marrow from organ donors, we can consistently optimize treatment outcomes.”

Warren Buffett marked another Thanksgiving by converting thousands of Berkshire Hathaway shares into a charitable donation valued at about $5.5 billion.
In a short annual Thanksgiving message released with the donation, the billionaire investor and businessman wrote that the most powerful returns in life aren’t measured in stock prices. “Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate.”
He converted 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares which were distributed to four Buffett family-led foundations. The gift continues his plan to give away essentially all of his shares of Berkshire Hathaway – the company he ran for more than 60 years.
Buffett directed the shares to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation , a major funder of reproductive health and Nebraska scholarships; the Nebraska-focused Sherwood Foundation , which supports education, human services, and community development in his home state; the Howard G. Buffett Foundation , which works on global food security, conflict mitigation, and anti-trafficking efforts; and the NoVo Foundation , which emphasizes gender equity, regenerative agriculture, and community resilience.
The roughly $5.5 billion Thanksgiving gift is substantially larger than the approximately $1.3 billion in shares he gave the same foundations last year, consistent with his goal of increasing the size of annual grants over time. He has said he intends to complete the transfer of his remaining Berkshire shares to the four foundations by the end of 2034. ⁠
Buffett also took a moment to thank those who helped him along the way to becoming one of the world’s richest men. “Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I’m grateful to every one of them,” Buffett wrote.
He left readers with a simple message for the season: Pay it forward.
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

items.text:
Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings saved from an approaching storm in California were released into the wild over the weekend.
It was late September when a female turtle climbed out of the sea, dug a nest on the beach, deposited her clutch, and slipped back into the water leaving nothing but a small trail in the sand and a couple of speechless lifeguards.
This first-ever instance of a turtle nesting on America’s Pacific coast was repeated a day later on Huntington Beach in what were the first ever recorded sea turtle nests on the West Coast.
After at first being left to incubate and hatch naturally, storm forecasts saw state and federal authorities evacuate the nests and take the eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.
The hatchlings emerged at the Aquarium and were quickly transported to Orange County beaches for release. Photos released by the Aquarium that were taken with red or infrared light show handlers measuring each hatchling before letting them scurry down to the water on their own, with minimal human disturbance and other distractions.
“It is not known why these sea turtles chose Southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it may indicate important historical changes that could have long-term implications for this species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” said Cassandra Davis, Director of Volunteer Services at the Aquarium, who said neither weather nor mere anomalous behavior were being ruled out as a theory.
Jonathan Snyder of the US Fish and Wildlife Service office in Carlsbad said another nest was recently documented further up the coast in Ventura County in November, and that it’s therefore unclear exactly how many turtles have nested in total.
He told reporters that one obvious potential reason for this never-before-witnessed event could be the Super El Niño weather phenomenon this year, though his overarching thoughts were positive.
“There have been decades of effort by dedicated individuals both in the US and abroad that have done everything they can for sea turtle conservation, and those efforts have really moved the needle for conservation for a variety of species, but for Olive Ridley sea turtles in particular,” said Snyder in a press conference.
“Their populations have increased substantially throughout portions of their range, and it’s the reason why there are these sea turtles along our coast that could take advantage of these unique environmental conditions.”

Your cat may be trying to tell you something with their meows, and you may not like what they’re saying. A new study from animal behavior researchers at the University of São Paulo in Brazil suggests that cats use their voices to actively seek help from their owners and communicate their needs . In other words, your cat might have a complaint, and you’re the one expected to fix it.
While we know cats to meow quite frequently, this is a behavior that our furry friends rarely use with one another, and feral cats meow even less. This points to the meow as a communication tool particularly suited to cat-human interactions, and the new study offers further evidence of this.
The researchers enlisted 38 pet cats who were known by their humans to be frequent meowers, particularly when food was involved. Then, the cats were given an extremely frustrating situation: their favorite treat was placed in a plastic box with holes, so they could smell the food but not reach it. Talk about torture. For one minute each, the researchers observed the cats’ behavior under two different circumstances. In one, the cat was alone with the box, and in the other, its human was present and paying attention. And this is where the behavior changed significantly.
If there was a human present watching the cat struggle, the cat was much more likely to use its voice to get their attention. The researchers recorded a total of 86 meows when a human was present, compared to just 20 when the cats were alone. They also used their eyes , often looking directly at their owners or alternating their gaze between the person and the food box, as though the message wasn’t already clear enough. items.title: How Did Ancient Egypt's Sacred Cats Live? More Than 100 Unwrapped Mummies Reveal Poor Living Conditions, Infections and Violence Before Death
items.desc: Osteological and chemical tests on 131 museum specimens reveal that domestic cats and wild-caught jungle cats later destined for mummification suffered high rates of disease and physical trauma
items.text:
Across ancient Egypt, millions of cats were once mummified and laid to rest in sprawling animal necropolises to honor the gods. Now, a closer look at more than a hundred preserved skulls reveals that these sacred animals endured surprisingly brutal lives.
Researchers analyzed 131 well-preserved cat skulls housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna that originally came from Beni Hassan , an ancient animal funerary site in Egypt’s Nile Valley, some 155 miles south of Cairo. The majority of skulls belonged to adult cats, mostly domestic and some wild. They were largely dated between 380 B.C.E. and 40 B.C.E Osteological and chemical examinations revealed widespread signs of gum disease, infections, healed wounds and fatal skull fractures, according to a study recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
“What struck us most was the high proportion of injuries and evidence of disease, suggesting that these cats lived in poor conditions,” Bea De Cupere , study co-author and archaeozoologist at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, tells Phys.org ’s Sandee Oster. “This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies.”
In ancient Egypt, cats were revered as earthly embodiments of the goddess Bastet and frequently appeared on tomb walls and artifacts. Eventually, devotees began mummifying felines as sacred offerings across at least 20 animal cemeteries in Egypt, according to the study.
In the 19th and early 20th centuries C.E., however, excavators were mostly interested in human mummies and used ancient animal remains as ship ballast, fuel, fertilizer or powdered medicine. The Beni Hassan skulls—the largest known museum collection of ancient Egyptian cat skulls with documented origin—survived only because British biologist William A. Herdman salvaged a small portion of roughly 200,000 animal mummies set out for a fertilizer auction in Liverpool in 1890, according to Gizmodo ’s Gayoung Lee. Since 19th-century scientists were mainly interested in skulls, the cats’ torsos were likely discarded after unwrapping.
To reconstruct the cats’ lives, lead author Wim Van Neer , also an archaeozoologist at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, and his team conducted X-ray and chemical isotope analyses alongside radiocarbon dating on nine of the skulls. In early November, several exhausted Kansas families touched down in Algeria at 4:30 a.m. and were shocked at what was waiting for them.
Dozens of representatives from the country’s government and hospitality sector were there, arms outstretched with flowers, happy to see them.
They had come to repay a debt to the travelers—a debt of kindness.
As dozens of international soccer teams descended on the United States for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, team Algeria chose Lawrence, Kansas—pop. 94.934. To the shock of the locals, hundreds of members of the North American Algerian diaspora, organized by a young woman attending the nearby University of Kansas, mobbed the small city and infected it with World Cup fever.

The heroic wartime bravery of a British shopkeeper who hid Allied commandos from the Nazis during WWII has been revealed 40 years after her death.
Ada Le Poidevin was living on the island of Guernsey in the English Channel when she sheltered three British soldiers left behind during a raid on the Nazi-occupied land in 1940.
Despite German troops living next door, she decided to help Corporal Dennis Dumper, Pvt. Fred Drain, and Pvt. Andrew Ross who were stranded without food or shelter.
Ada and her husband Walter offered their garden shed for them to hide in, despite severe consequences if the trio were to be discovered.
All three survived the conflict and they remained close to Ada and Walter, regularly returning to Guernsey to visit them and even attending the couple’s Golden Wedding celebration.
It was the second time Ada had put herself in danger during wartime. During WWI, she spent two years supporting British troops in France working in camps that came under enemy fire—and suffered heavy damage.
Now her story has been pieced together by her niece Liz Walton, using a treasure trove of diaries, photographs, and records she inherited.
“There were huge risks because there were Germans living next door and people were being sent off to concentration camps, said the 79-year-old Walton. “They were terrified of being caught.”
“It must have been absolutely horrendous for people like my aunt, who had been involved in the first World War, and then 20 years later to have the Germans actually in their homes.”
Liz, a retired teacher from Guernsey, turned into a detective to match her aunt’s personal accounts and photos with official wartime records.
She had been fascinated by Ada’s stories since childhood until she died at the age of 88—of ordinary people sacrificing during extraordinary times.
Ada was born in 1895 in Guernsey (30 miles west of the coastline of Normandy, France), and volunteered for the Salvation Army in France in 1917, while in her early 20s.
“There were no men in our family that could go and fight,” Liz said. “She felt a calling to go.”
Ada spent two years in British camps, providing refreshments to soldiers, writing letters for them, and mending their clothes—at sites being fired upon more than once.

What began as an exciting hiking trip quickly turned into something else entirely when climbers in Greece found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the bottom of a cliff.
Considered a Critically Endangered species in Greece, the climbers resolved to go right back up the way they came—the seal pup safely secured in a backpack.
It was stranded without its mother on the inaccessible Kalamia Beach—whose beauty and solitude were supposed to be the climbers’ reward for negotiating the rugged cliffs on the island of Kythira.
Vrettos Sklavos, from Outdoor Activities Greece said there is a sea cave near Kalamia Beach that these Mediterranean monk seals use to escape rough seas. Perhaps a big wave had separated the little fellow from its mother.
An animal rescue operation on the island wrote on Facebook that the climbers took “all the right steps,” calling (MOm) the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Mediterranean Monk Seal, the coast guard, and Animal Aid Kythira , whose veterinarians eventually descended the cliffs together with the climbers to rescue the seal.
“A huge thank you to Vrettos and his team for their immediate response,” the operation wrote on Facebook.
In an update from Keep Talking Greece , the seal is said to have arrived severely dehydrated and malnourished, weighing just 15 kilograms at 1 year old. It was determined that after a brief stay with Animal Aid Kythira it would be transported to Thessaly on the mainland before eventually arriving at the Society’s rehabilitation location in Spata.
Here, it will receive round-the-clock care with the aim of attempting to preserve enough of its wild intuition and nature as to permit a return to the sea when the time is right.

Exclusive: investigation finds prescriptions for children under 12, as experts stress need for specialist supervision and long-term monitoring
Hundreds of children in England are receiving prescriptions for GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12, the Guardian can reveal.
GLP-1 medications were initially developed to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels, but have since become a popular slimming aid, with products such as Wegovy and Mounjaro becoming household names.
While social media is awash with adults who have lost weight with GLP-1s, data shows a number of children are also being prescribed them.
A Guardian investigation has revealed that in the financial year 2025-26 there were 419 children under the age of 18 receiving such prescriptions, 10 of whom were under the age of 12. And in the four months to July this year, 341 children received GLP-1 prescriptions, 15 of whom were under the age of 12.
The figures, obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests, relate to prescriptions in England and dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK.
However, they do not cover those prescribed and dispensed via private prescriptions, in prisons, and in hospitals, meaning the figures are likely to be a considerable underestimate.
One private clinic for children has previously revealed it has more than 200 patients receiving the jabs. It is also unclear whether the GLP-1 figures reflect medications that are being given primarily for weight loss.
Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, said the number of prescriptions was still small relative to the scale of childhood obesity, but those taking the drugs needed long-term change to their lifestyles.
He said: “The important thing is that children who start them do so within specialist services, with support for diet, growth and wellbeing, and a plan for the long term.
“That includes regular monitoring of growth and puberty, nutritional intake, mental health and eating behaviours, and side effects. This matters partly because we know weight tends to return when the drugs are stopped, and partly because we still have limited data on use over many years in growing young people.”

items.title: Experts explore returning beavers to River Waveney
items.desc: A trust says the river-dwelling mammals could improve the health of the waterway.
items.text:
Beavers could be reintroduced to the River Waveney, like the ones pictured here, that have been living in the River Glaven, Norfolk
A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.
The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.
The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.
Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.
Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.
Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.
But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.
Two beaver babies - or kits - were born in the wild in Norfolk for the first time in 500 years at Pensthorpe Natural Park
Beavers have been reintroduced already in Norfolk at enclosures at Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve near Fakenham, Wild Ken Hill near King's Lynn and on the River Glaven near Holt.
A pair of beavers have also been spotted in the wild at Pensthorpe Natural Park, which is a short distance downstream from Sculthorpe Moor.
In Suffolk, a colony was introduced at Little Haugh Hall at Norton, near Bury St Edmunds.
River Waveney Trust is holding a series of events to discuss the proposals and it hopes to engage with local landowners in Bungay, Palgrave and Eye.
Lamb added: "Our aim is to ensure that local communities, landowners, anglers and conservation groups have the opportunity to be part of the discussion from the beginning."
While talks are beginning, Lamb said it would be years before any decision would be made, which would require a licence from Natural England.

items.title: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
items.desc: Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
items.text:
Spread by midges, bluetongue poses no threat to the public or food safety
The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.
Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.
The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.
The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.
The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than 100 cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months.
Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed.
There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland.
The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season.
Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to Daera.
"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety – milk and meat are safe to consume."
Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.
"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.
"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."
The disease was first detected in Northern Ireland near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.
A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.
Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.
The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.
